chief_complaint: profound coma immediately following high-speed motor vehicle collision with normal initial head CT
hpi_details: 29M post-MVC in deep coma (GCS 4) with normal initial CT but gradient-echo (GRE/SWI) MRI demonstrating punctate microhemorrhages at grey-white junction and corpus callosum.
ideas: His mother thinks he is in a deep sleep from the physical trauma and heavy hospital sedatives because his initial brain scan was normal.
concerns: His mother is terrified that he has hidden, irreversible brain damage and will never wake up to speak or walk again.
expectations: His mother hopes the doctors will explain why he is still unresponsive despite the clean scan and give her an honest timeline for his awakening.

available_results.value: No acute hemorrhage or mass effect
Numerous punctate microhemorrhages at the gray-white junction and within the corpus callosum
available_results.note: Pattern is consistent with severe diffuse axonal injury.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocols for diffuse axonal injury, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: profound coma immediately following high-speed motor vehicle collision with normal initial head CT
Key HPI features: 29M post-MVC in deep coma (GCS 4) with normal initial CT but gradient-echo (GRE/SWI) MRI demonstrating punctate microhemorrhages at grey-white junction and corpus callosum.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for diffuse axonal injury.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Epidural/subdural hematoma (would show on initial CT) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as deep coma (very low GCS) with a normal initial CT; this mismatch itself is a clue to DAI.
management_principles: Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocols for diffuse axonal injury
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: High-energy rotational forces from a crash shear brain axons throughout the white matter, causing deep coma despite a normal-looking initial CT scan; special MRI sequences can reveal the microscopic damage.
differentials: Epidural/subdural hematoma (would show on initial CT)
red_flags: Deep coma (very low GCS) with a normal initial CT; this mismatch itself is a clue to DAI

must_ask.say: For a witness: can you describe the accident, including the speed and type of impact?
How responsive has he been since the accident?
How long has he been unconscious?
What other injuries did he sustain in the crash?
What have you been told so far about his condition?

history.answer: My brother was in a severe car crash about an hour ago, and he has been completely unconscious and unresponsive ever since.
He was completely independent, active, and mentally sharp with no memory or thinking problems before this crash.
He lost consciousness instantly at the moment of the crash about an hour ago, and he has not woken up or shown any alertness since.
He is in a deep coma, does not open his eyes or respond when we shout his name, and has not spoken or had any hallucinations.
He was driving at high speed on the expressway when his car crashed head-on into another vehicle, causing massive front-end impact.
The collision occurred roughly an hour ago, and the ambulance rushed him straight here to the trauma center.
The paramedics said his seatbelt was buckled; he has scrapes on his forehead and chest, but no obvious deformed or broken limbs.
He cannot move or talk at all, and his arms and legs seem stiff rather than weak on one side.
He couldn't tell us if his head hurt because he went unconscious immediately, and he has not vomited.
He has not had any rhythmic shaking, tongue biting, or loss of bladder control, though his body sometimes stiffens up.
No, he had no fever, chills, cough, or painful urination in the days leading up to this accident.
He had no stiff neck, light sensitivity, or skin rash before the collision.
He does not have diabetes, does not use insulin or diabetes pills, and has never had low blood sugar episodes.
He was eating and drinking normally earlier today, with no diarrhea, vomiting, or signs of dehydration.
He takes no medications at all, so there were no new sleeping pills, painkillers, or prescription mistakes.
He does not drink alcohol or use recreational drugs, and police found no open bottles or pills in his car.
He is physically fit, well-nourished, and had no gait unsteadiness or double vision before the crash.
No, he was not exposed to any gas leaks, carbon monoxide, pesticides, or extreme heat.
He has no history of liver disease or kidney failure, and he has never looked yellow or swollen.
He has no history of depression, psychiatric conditions, or unexplained episodes of unresponsiveness.
Since the first CT scan came back clear, I thought he was just sleeping deeply from the shock of the car crash and pain medicine.
I'm terrified that his brain is permanently damaged and that my boy will never wake up or recognize us again.
I just need the doctor to explain why he won't wake up if the scan was clean and tell me when we might expect him to open his eyes.
He has no chronic medical illnesses and has always been in good health.
He has never undergone surgery and has never been admitted to a hospital.
He does not take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or dietary supplements.
He has no known allergies to any medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
He has never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine products.
He does not drink alcoholic beverages.
He works as a software engineer and lives in an apartment with his partner.
There is no family history of stroke, aneurysm, seizures, or early neurological disorders.

exam.finding: Young adult male lying supine in a rigid cervical collar, completely unresponsive to verbal commands with visible chest and forehead abrasions.
Blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and fingerstick blood glucose 108 mg/dL.
Deep coma with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 4 (E1V1M2), demonstrating no eye opening or verbalization, and extensor posturing to noxious stimulation.
Pupils are round, equal at 3 mm, and sluggishly reactive to light bilaterally without papilledema or retinal hemorrhage.
Bilateral corneal reflexes are blunted, oculocephalic responses are sluggish, and there is no facial asymmetry.
Increased tone across all four extremities with bilateral decerebrate posturing upon noxious stimulation; no spontaneous purposeful movements or unilateral hemiparesis.
Symmetrically brisk 3+ deep tendon reflexes throughout, with bilateral extensor plantar responses (positive Babinski signs).
Neck is maintained in cervical collar; no nuchal rigidity detected, and Kernig and Brudzinski signs are absent.
Superficial contusions and abrasions on the forehead and anterior chest wall consistent with a seatbelt mark, with no signs of basilar skull fracture or scalp lacerations.
Oral cavity is clear of blood, secretions, and foreign objects with no tongue lacerations or bite marks; airway is intact.
Sclerae are anicteric and conjunctivae are pink without pallor or petechiae.
